---
title: "The setlist is made of blocks"
subtitle: "Hierarchical cluster"
date: 2026-08-20
categories: [structure]
image: images/14-setlist-blocos.png
image-alt: "Cluster chart showing the three fixed blocks of a Paul McCartney setlist"
---

A Paul McCartney show feels spontaneous, three hours, decades of catalogue, no visible script. I ran a cluster analysis on the 13 setlists I've seen him play and found the opposite: a stable structure of blocks.

Distance between two songs is how far apart, on average, they sit in the set. Cluster them and three clean, contiguous blocks fall out: an opening run of upbeat hits, a long acoustic and deep-cut middle, and a fixed emotional closing block, Let It Be through the Abbey Road medley.

The closing block is the rigid one. Golden Slumbers, Carry That Weight and The End moved less than 5.3% of the set's length across 13 shows spanning 14 years. Three other songs (A Day in the Life, Paperback Writer, I've Got a Feeling) never found a stable slot at all, swinging from the opener to the encore depending on the night, and that inconsistency is exactly what proves the other blocks are real.

He isn't swapping songs. He's swapping modules, and one module never moves.

Any product built from swappable modules works the same way: some pieces are up for reshuffling, and one or two are load bearing.

Which part of your own routine never moves, no matter what else changes around it?
